passages.t: Timothy sent back to strengthen them
passages.happening:
“So when we could bear it no longer, we were willing to be left on our own in Athens. We sent Timothy, our brother and fellow worker for God in the gospel of Christ, to strengthen and encourage you in your faith, so that none of you would be shaken by these trials” (verses 1-3).

Paul reminds them that trouble was no surprise: “Indeed, when we were with you, we kept warning you that we would suffer persecution; and as you know, it has come to pass” (verse 4). “For this reason, when I could bear it no longer, I sent to find out about your faith, for fear that the tempter had somehow tempted you and caused our labor to be in vain” (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
Twice Paul says he ‘could bear it no longer’ (verses 1 and 5). He was anxious, and he says so. A church only weeks old had been left behind under pressure, and he had no way of knowing how it was doing.

There was no public post for private letters, and travel was slow and costly. To get news, Paul had to send someone he trusted, and that meant losing that person's help. So he sent Timothy and stayed in Athens alone. Acts says Paul found Athens “full of idols” (Acts 17:16). It was a lonely place to wait.

Acts does not mention this trip of Timothy's. It says Silas and Timothy were left in Berea and later came to Paul in Corinth (Acts 17:14-15; 18:5). The simplest way to put the two together is that Timothy came to Paul in Athens, was sent back north to Thessalonica, and later rejoined him in Corinth.

Timothy's job was ‘to strengthen and encourage’. The first word means to make firm, like setting a post solidly in the ground. The trials the Thessalonians faced were probably not soldiers sent by Rome. They were the hostility of neighbours, family and trade partners, who saw the new faith as a threat to the gods and to the city's peace. That kind of pressure can wear a person down slowly.

Paul's fear was ‘the tempter’. The Greek word can mean to test something to prove it, or to tempt someone to give up. Paul feared that under the strain they might have been lured away from faith, and that all the work would have come to nothing.
passages.ot:
Strengthening the weak is the work God gives his people. “Strengthen the limp hands and steady the feeble knees!” (Isaiah 35:3). Tell the anxious, ‘Be strong, do not fear’ (Isaiah 35:4). When David was hunted, “Saul’s son Jonathan came to David in Horesh and strengthened his hand in God” (1 Samuel 23:16). Timothy is sent to do what Jonathan did.

The hope that a believer will not be shaken is in the Psalms: “I have set the LORD always before me. Because He is at my right hand, I will not be shaken” (Psalm 16:8). “Those who trust in the LORD are like Mount Zion. It cannot be moved” (Psalm 125:1).

And the tempter is old. In the garden the serpent asked, “Did God really say” (Genesis 3:1). In Job, Satan wagers that suffering will make a faithful man curse God (Job 1:9-11). Paul feared that same voice in Thessalonica.
passages.hard:
Paul says ‘we are destined for this’, meaning trouble. Does God want his people to suffer?

Paul is not saying that suffering is good in itself, or that God delights in it. He is saying it should not surprise them. Jesus told his followers the same: “In the world you will have tribulation. But take courage; I have overcome the world!” (John 16:33). Following a crucified Lord in a world that resists him will bring trouble. Paul had warned them before it came, so that when it came they would not think God had left them.

That is the point. Trouble does not mean God has abandoned you, or that your faith has failed. Paul's response to their suffering was not to blame them. It was to send help, and to pray.

And this verse is about suffering for the faith. It is never a reason to tell someone who is being hurt by another person that they must stay and bear it. Nothing in this passage asks anyone to stay where they or their children are in danger. If you are being hurt, at home, at work or in a church, tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Paul could not bear not knowing how his friends were, so he gave up his own helper to find out. Ask whom you are anxious about, and whether there is someone you could send, or a call you could make. Ask who strengthened you when your faith was shaken. And if you are under pressure now, hear what Paul told them: this is not a sign that God has left you.

passages.t: Timothy's good news, and Paul's joy
passages.happening:
“But just now, Timothy has returned from his visit with the good news about your faith, your love, and the fond memories you have preserved, longing to see us just as we long to see you” (verse 6).

“For this reason, brothers, in all our distress and persecution, we have been reassured about you, because of your faith. For now we can go on living, as long as you are standing firm in the Lord” (verses 7-8).

“How can we adequately thank God for you in return for our great joy over you in His presence? Night and day we pray most earnestly that we may see you face to face and supply what is lacking from your faith” (verses 9-10).
passages.hearers:
You can feel the relief in these verses. The word Paul uses for Timothy's ‘good news’ is the word usually used for preaching the gospel. It is the only place in Paul's letters where he uses it for anything else. To Paul, the news that this little church was still standing was gospel-sized news.

Timothy brought three things: their faith, their love, and their warm memories of Paul. The Thessalonians had not decided that Paul was a fraud who had run away. They missed him as much as he missed them.

Verse 8 is one of the most open things Paul ever wrote. ‘Now we can go on living.’ It is as if his own life depended on their standing firm. That is how a parent feels about a child far away.

Notice that Paul himself was in ‘distress and persecution’ in Corinth. His own troubles were not over. But hearing that they were well lifted him.

And notice verse 10. Paul is overjoyed, but he does not say they are finished. He wants to ‘supply what is lacking’ in their faith. Their faith was real, and it was young. There was more to learn, and chapters 4 and 5 begin to supply it. Joy over someone's faith and care for its growth go together.
passages.ot:
Proverbs knew the feeling: “Like cold water to a weary soul is good news from a distant land” (Proverbs 25:25).

The psalmist asked Paul's question of thanks: “How can I repay the LORD for all His goodness to me?” (Psalm 116:12).

And standing firm in the Lord is the faith of the Psalms. “Those who trust in the LORD are like Mount Zion. It cannot be moved; it abides forever” (Psalm 125:1).
passages.asks: Paul says he can go on living because his friends are standing firm. Ask whose faith matters that much to you, and whether you pray for them night and day. Ask what news would bring you that kind of joy. And ask what is still lacking in your own faith, and who might help to supply it.

passages.t: A prayer for the road back, for love, and for holiness
passages.happening:
Paul turns his longing into a prayer. “Now may our God and Father Himself, and our Lord Jesus, direct our way to you” (verse 11).

“And may the Lord cause you to increase and overflow with love for one another and for everyone else, just as our love for you overflows, so that He may establish your hearts in blamelessness and holiness before our God and Father at the coming of our Lord Jesus with all His saints. Amen” (verses 12-13).
passages.hearers:
This prayer closes the first half of the letter, and it points to the second. Love for one another, and holiness, will be the subject of chapter 4. The coming of the Lord Jesus will fill the end of chapter 4 and the start of chapter 5.

Look at whom Paul prays to: ‘our God and Father Himself, and our Lord Jesus’. And in the Greek the verb ‘direct’ is singular, as though the Father and the Son act as one. Within twenty years of the resurrection, Jesus is being prayed to alongside the Father.

Paul prays for love that overflows, like a cup filled past the brim. And it is not only love ‘for one another’, inside the church. It is ‘for everyone else’ too, including, it must be said, the neighbours who were making their lives hard.

Then he prays that the Lord will ‘establish’ their hearts. It is the same word he used for Timothy's work in verse 2: to make firm. What Timothy began by encouraging, God will finish. The goal is a heart that is blameless and holy when Jesus comes. Paul does not pray that they will make themselves holy. He asks the Lord to do it.

‘With all His saints’. The word means ‘holy ones’. Readers differ on whether Paul means angels, or believers who have died, or both. Each reading has support, and nothing in the prayer depends on choosing.
passages.ot:
Verse 13 echoes Zechariah. The prophet said, “Then the LORD my God will come, and all the holy ones with Him” (Zechariah 14:5). Paul speaks of the coming of the Lord Jesus ‘with all His saints’. What Zechariah said of the LORD, Paul says of Jesus.

In the Old Testament ‘holy ones’ can mean the angels who surround God: “In the council of the holy ones, God is greatly feared” (Psalm 89:7). It can also mean God's people: “But the saints of the Most High will receive the kingdom and possess it forever” (Daniel 7:18).

And asking God to direct one's way is an old prayer: “The steps of a man are ordered by the LORD” (Psalm 37:23).
passages.asks: Paul prays for love that overflows, even toward people outside the church. Ask whom your love stops short of. Ask whether you pray for the people who make your life hard. And ask whether you trust God to make you holy, or think it is all up to you.
